| Employee | Likely submitted code | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Leanne Cartwright | SC | Unchanged; she notified the team early and reported flu. |
| Mohammed Iqbal | DEP | His daughter needed emergency care because her school closed. |
| Ryan Whitaker | UA, with an explanatory note | His absence does not fit SC, DEP or BRV under the stated definitions. |
| Karen Dobson | UA | Unchanged; no explanation or notification was given. |
| Paul Hendry | SC, probably with a note | A routine dental appointment would probably be treated as a self-certified medical absence by an ordinary employee, although a strictly literal reading might leave it as UA. |

For Ryan, the employee would probably try to contact Gary or escalate the matter, but neither Gary nor the HR Manager is available before payroll. They might feel that invoking the second-UA rule is unfair because Ryan called at 05:40 and had a genuine family emergency. Nevertheless, under the supplied definitions:

- he was not ill, so SC does not apply;
- his sister was not his spouse, child, parent or household resident, so DEP does not apply;
- there was no death, so BRV does not apply; and
- annual leave cannot be booked retrospectively.

Thus the most defensible prediction is that he remains coded UA, with a note recording the labour, the hospital visit and his 05:40 call. Because he already had a UA on 18 August, that would cause the payroll system to issue the probation-termination letter that day. The note would preserve the explanation but would not prevent the action.

A less rule-bound human might instead stretch DEP or leave Ryan’s original SC code to avoid triggering the letter. That is quite possible, but I would predict the documented codes and the fixed payroll deadline make the stricter classification more likely.
